questions.q: On which layer of the Earth do we live?
questions.a: the crust

questions.q: According to the chapter, who gave the theory of plate tectonics, which explains the movement of the Earth's crust?
questions.a: W.J. Morgan

questions.q: Fig. 2.1 gives the outer core as about 2200 km thick and the inner core as about 1250 km thick. About how thick is the whole core, outer and inner together?
questions.a: about 3450 km

questions.q: A town stands on a tectonic plate that moves 5 cm every year. If the plate keeps this speed, how many years will it take for the town to be carried 1 km?
questions.a: 20,000 years

questions.q: Name the three main types of tectonic plates and say what each type carries.
questions.a: Continental plates carry continents, oceanic plates carry ocean floors, and mixed plates carry both continents and oceans.
s: Names continental, oceanic and mixed plates
States that they carry continents, ocean floors, and both, respectively

questions.q: True or False: Tectonic plates do not all move in the same direction, because convection currents in the mantle both push and pull them.
questions.a: True. Heat from the core makes molten material in the mantle rise while cooler material sinks; the convection currents this creates push and pull the plates, so they move in different directions.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rising hot and sinking cool material form convection currents that push and pull the plates in different directions

questions.q: Using the descriptions in Fig. 2.1, write one feature of each of these layers: (a) the outer core, (b) the inner core, (c) the asthenosphere.
questions.a: (a) The outer core is a fluid layer made mainly of iron and nickel. (b) The inner core is a solid, hot, spinning metal ball and the densest part of the Earth. (c) The asthenosphere is a hot, mobile layer of partially molten rock.
s: Outer core: fluid layer, mainly iron and nickel
Inner core: solid, hot, spinning metal ball, densest part of the Earth
Asthenosphere: hot, mobile, partially molten rock

questions.q: Take the lithosphere as 100 km thick everywhere, the continental crust as 30 km and the oceanic crust as 5 km, as in Fig. 2.1. (a) Under a continent, how many km of the lithosphere is upper mantle? (b) Under an ocean, how many km of it is upper mantle? (c) What does this show about which part makes up most of the lithosphere under the oceans?
questions.a: (a) 100 - 30 = 70 km of upper mantle. (b) 100 - 5 = 95 km of upper mantle. (c) Under the oceans the crust is only 5 km of the 100 km (5%), so the lithosphere there is almost all upper mantle; the lithosphere is the crust together with the upper part of the mantle, not the crust alone.
s: Continent: 100 - 30 = 70 km of upper mantle
Ocean: 100 - 5 = 95 km of upper mantle
Concludes the oceanic lithosphere is almost all upper mantle (crust only 5%), so the lithosphere is crust plus upper mantle

questions.q: Answer each part in one line. (a) Name the three main layers of the Earth. (b) What two parts together form the lithosphere? (c) Name the layer beneath the lithosphere that allows the plates to move, and say what it is like. (d) The chapter gives the crust as 30-40 km thick under continents and 5-7 km under the ocean. By how many km is the thinnest continental crust thicker than the thickest oceanic crust? (e) What causes the plates to move?
questions.a: (a) Crust, mantle and core. (b) The crust and the upper part of the mantle. (c) The asthenosphere, which is semi-molten. (d) 30 - 7 = 23 km. (e) Convection currents in the mantle, set up by heat from the core.
s: Crust, mantle and core
Crust and upper mantle form the lithosphere
Asthenosphere, semi-molten
Convection currents in the mantle

questions.q: Two research teams want to drill through the crust to reach the mantle. Team Land will drill from a plain in the middle of a continent. Team Sea will drill from a ship, starting at the sea floor. Both rigs drill 2 km of rock a year, and drilling costs Rs 10 crore for every km. Team Sea must also hire its ship, which costs an extra Rs 60 crore for every year at sea. Use the crust thicknesses the chapter gives for continents and for oceans. (a) Which team has the thinner crust to cross, and what range does the chapter give for it? (b) What is the least depth each team must drill to reach the mantle? (c) Using those least depths, how many years will each team take, and what will each spend in all? (d) The funding body can pay for only one team. Which should it choose? Justify your choice with your answers.
questions.a: (a) Team Sea: the crust under the ocean is 5-7 km thick, against 30-40 km under continents. (b) At least 5 km for Team Sea and at least 30 km for Team Land. (c) Team Sea: 5 / 2 = 2.5 years; 5 x 10 + 2.5 x 60 = 50 + 150 = Rs 200 crore. Team Land: 30 / 2 = 15 years; 30 x 10 = Rs 300 crore. (d) Team Sea: the ship makes each year at sea costly, but the crust is so much thinner that it still finishes in one-sixth of the time and for Rs 100 crore less; even at the full 7 km it needs only 3.5 years and 70 + 210 = Rs 280 crore, still below Team Land's least cost.
s: (a) Team Sea; oceanic crust 5-7 km (continental 30-40 km)
(b) Least depths: 5 km at sea, 30 km on land
(c) Sea: 2.5 years, Rs 200 crore (including the ship); Land: 15 years, Rs 300 crore
(d) Chooses Team Sea, weighing the ship's yearly cost against the much thinner crust, using the figures

questions.q: At which type of plate boundary do two plates move away from each other?
questions.a: a divergent boundary

questions.q: Match each place or feature in Column I with what the chapter says about it in Column II. Column I: 1. The Himalaya  2. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge  3. The San Andreas Fault  4. Baratang Island. Column II: (a) plates slide past each other, mainly causing earthquakes  (b) mud bubbles out because of underground gases and pressure  (c) fold mountains formed where continental plates collide  (d) magma rises and forms new crust where plates move apart

Read the statements. Statement I: At a transform boundary, crust is neither created nor destroyed. Statement II: When an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate, the continental plate sinks beneath the oceanic plate. Statement III: The area around the Pacific Ocean where most earthquakes and volcanoes occur is called the Ring of Fire. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: Two places are struck by earthquakes of the same strength: a thinly populated desert and a crowded city. Which reason, based on the chapter, best explains why the city suffers far greater loss?
questions.a: Many more people and buildings are exposed to the shaking in a densely populated place.
o: Many more people and buildings are exposed to the shaking in a densely populated place.
An earthquake releases more energy under a city than an earthquake of the same strength under a desert.
The city must lie closer to a plate boundary than the desert, so it shakes for longer.
The city must lie in the Ring of Fire, while deserts are never close to plate boundaries.

questions.q: (a) What are plate boundaries? (b) Name the type of plate boundary at which plates slide past each other.
questions.a: (a) Plate boundaries are the edges where tectonic plates meet. (b) A transform boundary.
s: Edges where tectonic plates meet
Transform boundary

questions.q: (a) What were earthquakes called in early times in India, and what does the word mean? (b) In which text did Varahamihira dedicate a section to earthquakes?
questions.a: (a) Bhukampa, meaning the shaking of the Earth. (b) The Brihatsamhita.
s: Bhukampa, the shaking of the Earth
Brihatsamhita

questions.q: The chapter says that plate tectonics plays a major role in shaping the Earth's surface. Give three things that the movement of plates leads to or explains.
questions.a: Any three: the formation of mountains, valleys, ocean basins, volcanoes and earthquakes, and the distribution of continents and oceans across the Earth.
s: First result, e.g. formation of mountains
Second result, e.g. volcanoes and earthquakes
Third result, e.g. ocean basins, valleys, or the distribution of continents and oceans

questions.q: Ravi says, 'New crust is made at every plate boundary; that is why the Earth's surface keeps changing.' How far is he right? Use the three types of boundary in your answer.
questions.a: He is only partly right. The surface does keep changing, but new crust is made only at divergent boundaries, where magma rises and forms mid-ocean ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At transform boundaries the plates slide past without creating or destroying crust, and at convergent boundaries plates move towards each other: continental plates fold into mountains like the Himalaya, and an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate.
s: Divergent boundary: new crust forms as magma rises (Mid-Atlantic Ridge)
Transform: no crust created or destroyed; convergent: plates collide or an oceanic plate sinks
Verdict: partly right; the surface changes, but new crust forms only at divergent boundaries

questions.q: Three places are being studied. Place P lies where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate. Place Q lies on a transform boundary. Place R lies in the middle of a plate, far from any boundary. (a) What happens to the plates at P, and what two kinds of event can this lead to? (b) What is the main event at Q, and why is no volcano or ridge built there? (c) Which place is least likely to have earthquakes and volcanoes? Give the chapter's reason. (d) Which of P and Q is more likely to see volcanic activity? Justify. (e) How does this comparison support the statement 'Plate movements are responsible for the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes'?
questions.a: (a) At P the oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate, leading to volcanic activity and earthquakes. (b) At Q the plates slide past each other, mainly causing earthquakes; no crust is created or destroyed, so no ridge or volcano is built. (c) R, because most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries and R is far from any boundary. (d) P, because the sinking oceanic plate leads to volcanic activity, while Q only has plates sliding past. (e) Events are concentrated where plates meet (P and Q) and rare where they do not (R), and the kind of event depends on how the plates move, so the movement of plates decides where earthquakes and volcanoes occur.
s: (a) Oceanic plate sinks beneath continental plate; volcanic activity and earthquakes
(b) Plates slide past, mainly earthquakes; no crust created or destroyed
(c) R, since most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries
(d) P, because of the sinking oceanic plate
(e) Events cluster at boundaries and their kind depends on plate movement

questions.q: A Class 9 group marks the 20 strongest earthquakes of one year on an outline world map. 13 lie in a belt around the edge of the Pacific Ocean; 4 lie along the Himalaya, where two continental plates collide; 2 lie along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; and 1 lies in the middle of a plate, far from any boundary. (a) What name does the chapter give to the belt around the Pacific Ocean? (b) What percentage of the 20 earthquakes lie along plate boundaries? (c) What type of boundary is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and what does magma do there? (d) The group must choose which statement its map supports better: X, 'Earthquakes occur only on plate boundaries', or Y, 'Most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries'. Which should it choose? Justify with the data.
questions.a: (a) The Ring of Fire. (b) 13 + 4 + 2 = 19 of 20, so 19 / 20 x 100 = 95%. (c) A divergent boundary: the plates move apart, and magma rises from below and forms new crust. (d) Statement Y: 19 of the 20 (95%) lie along boundaries, which matches the chapter's 'most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries'; but 1 earthquake lies far from any boundary, so 'only' in Statement X is not supported.
s: (a) Ring of Fire
(c) Divergent; magma rises and forms new crust
(d) Chooses Y: 95% on boundaries, but the one mid-plate earthquake rules out 'only'

questions.q: In a cold desert, rocks are heated by day and cooled sharply at night, and over the years they crack into smaller pieces that stay where they are. Which process is this?
questions.a: physical weathering

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the main agents of gradation named in the chapter?
questions.a: volcanoes

questions.q: Match each type of erosion in Column I with its description in Column II. Column I: 1. Water erosion  2. Wind erosion  3. Glacial erosion  4. Coastal erosion. Column II: (a) common in dry and sandy areas  (b) sea waves wear away the land along the shore  (c) caused by rivers, rain or ocean waves  (d) moving ice scrapes and carries rocks

Assertion (A): The Zabo system of Nagaland helps conserve soil and water on hillslopes. Reason (R): The Arthashastra contains detailed guidelines on land assessment and categorisation based on fertility and productivity. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: What is bunding? State one way in which it helps a farmer.
questions.a: Bunding is the building of earthen embankments along contour lines. It slows surface run-off, so less soil is eroded and more water soaks in, raising soil moisture.
s: Earthen embankments built along contour lines
One benefit: slows run-off, reduces soil erosion, or increases infiltration and soil moisture

questions.q: True or False: The agents of gradation only wear down high areas of land; they do not fill up low areas.
questions.a: False. The agents of gradation wear down, transport and deposit material, so they lower high areas and also fill up low areas, levelling the surface over time.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: they wear down, transport and deposit, lowering high areas and filling up low areas

questions.q: Name the three main types of weathering and give one cause of each.
questions.a: Physical weathering, caused by temperature changes, frost or wind; chemical weathering, caused by reactions of minerals with water, air or acids; biological weathering, caused by plants, animals or micro-organisms, such as roots growing into cracks.
s: Physical weathering with a cause (temperature change, frost or wind)
Chemical weathering with a cause (reaction with water, air or acids)
Biological weathering with a cause (plants, animals or micro-organisms)

questions.q: Name the conservation practice from the chapter that suits each case, and say what it does there. (i) Farmers on a steep hillside want to grow crops on a series of level steps. (ii) A small stream rushes down a slope after rain, carrying soil away. (iii) On a hillside, villagers want to dig trenches that hold rainwater and let it soak in.
questions.a: (i) Terracing: level or gently sloping steps on the hillside prevent soil erosion. (ii) A check dam across the stream: it reduces water velocity, prevents soil erosion and lets sediment settle. (iii) Contouring, with continuous contour trenches dug along the contour lines to slow, hold and infiltrate rainwater.
s: (i) Terracing, with what it does
(ii) Check dam, with what it does
(iii) Contouring / continuous contour trenches, with what it does

questions.q: Compare weathering and erosion. (a) What happens to the rock in each? (b) Does the material move in each? (c) Name the agents or causes of each. (d) Give one example of each. (e) Explain how the two work together to shape landforms over long periods.
questions.a: (a) In weathering, rocks break down into smaller pieces; in erosion, soil, rock and other surface material are worn away. (b) Weathering does not move the broken material; erosion carries it from one place to another. (c) Weathering: temperature changes, frost, wind, water, air, acids, plants, animals or micro-organisms; erosion: water, wind, ice and waves. (d) Plant roots splitting rock is weathering; wind carrying sand in a dry area is erosion. (e) Weathering breaks the rock and erosion removes it, so together they wear down mountains, carve valleys, form plains and create caves, cliffs and deltas.
s: (a) Weathering breaks rock; erosion wears it away
(b) Weathering does not move material; erosion carries it
(c) Causes of weathering and agents of erosion
(d) One correct example of each
(e) Together they wear down mountains, carve valleys and form plains, caves, cliffs, deltas

questions.q: A hillside farm has topsoil 30 cm deep. Without any protection, erosion removes 1.5 cm of topsoil every year. With bunding along the contour lines, the loss falls to 0.5 cm a year. Crops start failing once less than 15 cm of topsoil is left. (i) How many years until the crops start failing without protection? (ii) How many years with bunding? (iii) Using the chapter, explain why bunding slows the loss. (iv) Bunding costs money and labour. Is it worth it for this farm? Justify.
questions.a: (i) The farm can lose 30 - 15 = 15 cm; 15 / 1.5 = 10 years. (ii) 15 / 0.5 = 30 years. (iii) The earthen bunds along the contour lines slow surface run-off, so less soil is washed away and more water soaks in. (iv) Yes: bunding gives the farm three times as long (30 years instead of 10) before crops fail, and erosion of topsoil lowers yields, so the cost is repaid by the crops saved, though the farmer may still need other measures later.
s: (i) 15 cm can be lost; 15 / 1.5 = 10 years
(iii) Bunds slow run-off, reducing soil loss and increasing infiltration
(iv) Judges it worth it using the 10 versus 30 years and the loss of yield from eroded topsoil

questions.q: In which course of a river does it start to meander and form oxbow lakes and floodplains?
questions.a: the middle course
o: at the mouth of the river

questions.q: Assertion (A): Deltas are ideal for agriculture and support crops such as rice and jute. Reason (R): Deltas are highly fertile because of their rich alluvial soil. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: A waterfall forms where soft rock lies on top and hard rock lies below. Statement II: A meander forms through lateral erosion and the deposition of sediments. Statement III: Deltas are important for fishing because fresh water and salt water mix there. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: Near the end of its journey, a river is carrying a large load of sediment and its water is slowing down on almost flat land. What is it most likely to do here?
questions.a: Deposit large amounts of sediment, forming landforms such as deltas, levees and alluvial fans
o: Deposit large amounts of sediment, forming landforms such as deltas, levees and alluvial fans
Cut a deep V-shaped valley with strong erosion
Form waterfalls and rapids as the water speeds up
Carve cirques and aretes as it scrapes the land

questions.q: (a) What is a waterfall? (b) Give one way in which waterfalls are useful to people.
questions.a: (a) A waterfall is a landform where a river flows over a steep cliff or vertical drop. (b) Any one: they attract tourists and help the local economy; they can be used for hydroelectric power; they offer trekking and photography; they may hold cultural or religious significance.
s: River flowing over a steep cliff or vertical drop
One use: tourism, hydroelectric power, recreation, or cultural/religious significance

questions.q: A planner says, 'A meandering river is of no use to people, so no village should grow near one.' Use the chapter's account of meanders to judge the claim, giving two points.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Any two: the fertile soil deposited along the banks of meanders supports agriculture; villages and towns often develop on the gentle slopes near meanders; meandering rivers can be used for navigation, irrigation and, in some cases, tourism (the Grand Anicut or Kallanai shows a river used for irrigation).
s: Judges the claim wrong, with one use of meanders (e.g. fertile soil for farming)
A second use (settlement on gentle slopes, navigation, irrigation or tourism)

questions.q: Near the sea, a river splits into many smaller channels with low islands of sediment between them. (a) Name the landform, and the name Fig. 2.12 gives to the smaller channels. (b) Explain why the islands of sediment form here. (c) A builder says the islands are permanent, dry land and perfectly safe for a new town. Use the chapter to judge his claim.
questions.a: (a) A delta; the smaller channels are distributaries. (b) At its mouth the river slows down and deposits the sediment it has carried from upstream; the deposits build up into islands and bars. (c) He is wrong to call it perfectly safe: deltas do support dense settlement and trade, but the chapter says they can be prone to flooding, which affects human life.
s: (a) Delta; distributaries
(b) River slows at its mouth and deposits the sediment it carried
(c) Rejects 'perfectly safe': deltas are prone to flooding, though they support settlement

questions.q: A district wants to make better use of three river landforms it has: a waterfall in the hills, meanders in the plains and a delta near the sea. Using the chapter, state one use of the waterfall, one use of the meanders and one use of the delta, and name one crop that the delta can support.
questions.a: Waterfall: tourism, or hydroelectric power from the force of the falling water. Meanders: farming on the fertile soil deposited along their banks (also navigation, irrigation or settlement). Delta: agriculture on rich alluvial soil, fishing, or trade and transport. Crop: rice or jute.
s: One use of the waterfall
One use of the meanders
One use of the delta
Rice or jute

questions.q: Early agricultural societies and cities grew up along rivers such as the Ganga, the Nile and the Indus. Explain why, by answering these: (i) Which work of a river builds fertile plains? (ii) Name two landforms of the lower course built in this way. (iii) Give one way in which rivers help trade and transport. (iv) Give one risk that living on a delta brings.
questions.a: (i) Deposition: as the river loses energy it deposits sediment, building fertile land. (ii) Any two of deltas, levees and alluvial fans (floodplains also form in the middle course). (iii) Rivers provide navigable routes, so deltas become centres of trade and transportation. (iv) Deltas can be prone to flooding, which affects human life and activities.
s: (i) Deposition of sediment builds fertile plains
(ii) Two of deltas, levees, alluvial fans
(iii) Rivers give navigable routes for trade and transport
(iv) Flooding of deltas

questions.q: A survey team follows one river from the hills to the sea. Station A is 1,800 m above sea level; the river is narrow and fast and drops over a cliff of hard rock. Station B, 150 km downstream, is 300 m above sea level; the river winds in large loops and a curved lake lies cut off beside it. Station C, a further 590 km downstream, is 5 m above sea level, where the river splits into many channels. (a) Name the course of the river at each station. (b) Find the average fall in height per km from A to B, and from B to C. (c) How many times steeper is the A to B stretch than the B to C stretch? (d) Use your answers to explain why erosion is strongest near A and deposition is greatest near C.
questions.a: (a) A: upper course; B: middle course; C: lower course. (b) A to B: (1800 - 300) / 150 = 10 m per km; B to C: (300 - 5) / 590 = 0.5 m per km. (c) 10 / 0.5 = 20 times steeper. (d) The steep gradient near A gives the water strong erosive force, cutting V-shaped valleys and waterfalls; on the gentle gradient near C the river slows, loses energy and deposits large amounts of sediment, forming a delta.
s: (a) Upper, middle and lower courses
(b) 10 m per km and 0.5 m per km
(c) 20 times steeper
(d) Steep gradient gives strong erosion; gentle gradient slows the river so it deposits

questions.q: A beach is created mainly by
questions.a: the deposition of sediments by waves
o: the deposition of sediments by waves

questions.q: In a desert, a tourist picks up a rock whose faces have been polished and shaped by wind-blown sand. What is such a rock called?
questions.a: a ventifact

questions.q: Match each agent in Column I with a landform it makes in Column II. Column I: 1. Sea waves  2. Glaciers  3. Wind  4. Underground water. Column II: (a) barchan dune  (b) sinkhole  (c) sea cave  (d) cirque
Assertion (A): Fjords are used for harbours and fishing. Reason (R): Fjords are wide, shallow bays formed by wind erosion along desert coasts. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Give two ways in which caves and underground rivers are important for people, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Any two: they provide sources of fresh water; they offer tourism opportunities; some have cultural or religious significance.
s: First way, e.g. source of fresh water
Second way, e.g. tourism or cultural/religious significance

questions.q: True or False: Karst topography is formed mainly by wind erosion in sandy deserts.
questions.a: False. Karst topography is formed by underground water in areas of limestone or other soluble rocks, through chemical weathering and erosion.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: formed by underground water in limestone or soluble rock, by chemical weathering and erosion

questions.q: Name three landforms made by wind erosion and describe each in one line.
questions.a: Any three: yardangs, streamlined rock ridges carved by wind; ventifacts, rocks polished and shaped by sandblasting; deflation hollows or blowouts, shallow depressions where loose material is removed; desert pavements, flat surfaces left after finer particles are blown away.
s: First landform with its description
Second landform with its description
Third landform with its description

questions.q: A rocky headland sticks out into the sea near a fishing town. Waves have undercut its base, leaving a steep rock face. At the foot of this face is a flat rock area that is uncovered at low tide. On both sides of the headland, waves have hollowed out caves in weak parts of the rock, and last year the two caves met, making an opening right through the headland. Visitors now come by boat to see it. (a) Name the steep rock face. (b) Name the flat rock area at its foot. (c) Name the opening through the headland. (d) Give one way in which such coastal landforms influence human activities, as the chapter says.
questions.a: (a) A sea cliff. (b) A wave-cut (shore) platform. (c) A sea arch. (d) Some such coasts are important for tourism, while others need coastal protection to safeguard settlements.
s: (a) Sea cliff
(b) Wave-cut platform
(c) Sea arch
(d) Tourism, or coastal protection for settlements

questions.q: A coastal town has a line of sand dunes 2.5 km long between the sea and 600 houses. A builder offers the town Rs 30 lakh to dig out the sand from 1 km of the dunes for construction. The fishermen's association objects. (a) Which agent forms dunes, and where does the chapter say they are found? (b) Which use of dunes named in the chapter matters most to the 600 houses, and which use is the builder relying on? (c) What percentage of the dune line would be removed, and how long a line would be left? (d) Should the town accept the offer? Justify your decision using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Wind forms dunes, in desert areas or along sandy coasts. (b) For the houses: dunes protect coastal settlements from strong sea winds and waves. The builder relies on the use of dune sand for construction. (c) 1 / 2.5 = 40% removed, leaving 1.5 km. (d) It should refuse (or accept only a far smaller amount): the Rs 30 lakh is a one-time gain, but removing 40% of the barrier leaves part of the 600 houses exposed to sea winds and waves; sand for construction is a real use, but here the protection matters more.
s: (a) Wind; deserts or sandy coasts
(b) Protection of coastal settlements from sea winds and waves; sand for construction
(c) 40% removed, 1.5 km left
(d) Decision weighing the one-time payment against lost protection for the houses

questions.q: At the end of a glacier in a mountain valley, a ridge of debris has dammed a lake holding 60,00,000 cubic metres of water. A village below wants to use the lake for irrigation. One hectare of crops needs 5,000 cubic metres of water in a season, and the village plans to use 40% of the lake's water each season. (a) What is the debris that a glacier leaves behind called, and how does a medial moraine form? (b) Give two ways in which moraines are useful to people. (c) How many hectares can the village irrigate in a season? (d) Which type of moraine is holding this lake, and why is it useful for this plan? (e) Should the village depend on this lake? Give a judgement with one reason for and one caution.
questions.a: (a) Till; a medial moraine forms when two glaciers meet and their lateral moraines join in the middle. (b) Any two: they create fertile soil for agriculture; they form natural dams and lakes used for water supply, irrigation and sometimes hydroelectric power. (c) 40% of 60,00,000 = 24,00,000 cubic metres; 24,00,000 / 5,000 = 480 hectares. (d) A terminal moraine, found at the end of a glacier; it acts as a natural dam that holds the lake, so water is stored for irrigation without building a dam. (e) It can use the lake, since 480 hectares is a large area and glaciers are a crucial source of fresh water, but with caution: the dam is only loose moraine, so the village should not rely on it alone and should watch the water level.
s: (a) Till; medial moraine forms where two glaciers' lateral moraines join
(b) Two uses of moraines
(d) Terminal moraine, acting as a natural dam holding the water
(e) Judgement with one reason for and one caution

questions.q: Which of these is a NATURAL cause of landslides named in the chapter?
questions.a: heavy and continuous rainfall

questions.q: Where are dust storms common, according to the chapter?
questions.a: in desert and semi-arid regions where the soil is loose and dry
o: in desert and semi-arid regions where the soil is loose and dry
in dense rainforests with heavy rainfall
in marshy deltas with wet soil

questions.q: Assertion (A): Avalanches are caused only by natural factors; human activity plays no part in them. Reason (R): Heavy snowfall within a short period adds extra weight to the snowpack and makes it unstable. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: A sudden rise in temperature can partly melt snow and reduce the friction that holds it together. Statement II: Heavy rainfall cannot add water to a glacial lake; only melting glaciers can raise its level. Statement III: The natural dams that hold back glacial lakes are made of solid bedrock. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only

questions.q: Name the disaster described in each case. (a) Snow suddenly slides down a steep mountain slope. (b) Water is suddenly released from a lake held back by ice or loose moraine, flooding the valley below. (c) Strong winds lift loose, dry soil and sand high into the air.
questions.a: (a) An avalanche. (b) A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF). (c) A dust storm.
s: (a) Avalanche
(b) Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF)
(c) Dust storm

questions.q: A hill town shows four conditions: (i) a steep slope of loose, weathered rock; (ii) a new road cut into the foot of the slope; (iii) forest cleared on the slope above; (iv) drains that are blocked. Sort the four into natural and human causes of landslides, explain how condition (iv) can lead to a sudden slope failure, and say which condition the town cannot remove.
questions.a: Natural: (i) the steep slope of loose, weathered rock. Human: (ii) road construction, (iii) deforestation and (iv) poor drainage. Blocked drains let excess water collect in the soil and rock, which adds weight and reduces friction until the slope suddenly fails. The town cannot remove (i), the steep slope and loose rock; it can act on the other three.
s: Sorts (i) as natural and (ii), (iii), (iv) as human
Blocked drains let excess water accumulate, adding weight and reducing friction, so the slope fails suddenly
Names (i) as the one the town cannot remove

questions.q: In a semi-arid district, grass and tree cover fell from 60% of the land in 2010 to 35% in 2025 because of overgrazing. Over the same years, the number of dust-storm days rose from 8 to 20 a year. (i) By how many percentage points did the cover fall? (ii) By what percentage did the number of dust-storm days rise? (iii) Use the chapter to explain how the fall in cover can lead to more dust storms. (iv) The district can afford only one step: controlling grazing so that grass and trees can grow back, or putting up sirens that warn villages when a dust storm is coming. Which should it choose? Justify.
questions.a: (i) 60 - 35 = 25 percentage points. (ii) (20 - 8) / 8 x 100 = 150%. (iii) Sparse vegetation leaves the loose, dry soil exposed, so strong winds can lift it more easily. (iv) Controlling grazing: overgrazing is a cause the chapter names for sparse vegetation, so restoring cover tackles a cause and can cut the number of storm days; sirens only help people shelter and leave the storms as frequent as before, though drought and climate change will still bring some storms.
s: (i) 25 percentage points
(iii) Sparse vegetation exposes loose, dry soil to strong winds
(iv) Chooses grazing control as tackling a named cause, while sirens only warn

questions.q: The chapter links rising temperatures or climate change to some landform disasters. (a) How do rising temperatures increase the risk of a GLOF? (b) How can a sudden rise in temperature set off an avalanche? (c) How can climate change affect dust storms? (d) Which of the four disasters (landslides, avalanches, GLOFs, dust storms) is NOT linked to rising temperature or climate change in the causes the chapter gives? (e) Judge the statement: 'A warmer climate will raise the risk of landform disasters in high mountain areas.' Use your answers.
questions.a: (a) Rapid melting of glaciers increases the size and water level of glacial lakes, putting pressure on their natural dams of ice or loose moraine until they may collapse. (b) A sudden rise in temperature partly melts the snow, reducing the friction that holds it together. (c) Climate change and extreme weather can increase the frequency and intensity of dust storms. (d) Landslides: their causes in the chapter are heavy rain, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, steep slopes, loose rock and human activities, not rising temperature or climate change (avalanches and GLOFs are linked to rising temperature, dust storms to climate change). (e) Largely true: in high mountains warming raises the risk of both GLOFs and avalanches, though landslides there depend on other causes such as heavy rain and human activity.
s: (a) Glacier melt raises lake levels and pressure on ice or moraine dams
(b) Partial melting reduces friction holding snow together
(c) Climate change can raise the frequency and intensity of dust storms
(d) Landslides
(e) Judgement using GLOFs and avalanches, noting landslides have other causes
